claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is in an as-synthesized hierarchical heterostructure state.
SEM/EBSD imaging can provide the phase-size distributions, interfacial characteristics, and grain-boundary networks needed by the proposed model.

Integrating machine learning, microstructural imaging descriptors, and a physics-guided finite-element model will improve prediction of HfNbTiVAl10 tensile behavior relative to established full-scale simulations.
The proposed framework can forecast Young's modulus for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework can forecast yield strength for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework can forecast fracture-initiation behavior for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will reduce simulation runtime by approximately 50% relative to traditional full-scale finite-element simulations.
The proposed framework will improve predictive accuracy by 20–30% relative to traditional full-scale simulations.
Prediction errors will be within ±10% for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related metrics.
Phase-size distribution, interfacial character, and grain-boundary networks mediate the relationship between HfNbTiVAl10's hierarchical heterostructure and its elastic and fracture behavior.
A convolutional neural network can extract complex microstructural features from imaging data.
The extracted microstructural features will be used as input descriptors in a physics-informed finite-element model.
Focusing simulations on critical microstructural parameters reduces the simulation search space.
Reducing the simulation search space accelerates prediction of elastic modulus, yield strength, and fracture-initiation sites.
Conventional finite-element methods currently used for HfNbTiVAl10 have longer runtimes and potentially larger prediction errors.
Predictive improvements may fail when imaging omits critical local features or when loading conditions are far outside the calibration range.
An insufficiently comprehensive training dataset or unresolved microstructural features may limit model generalizability.
Systematic errors greater than ±10% for any target parameter across a statistically significant independent sample set will falsify the hypothesis.
